public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Reaction performance depends categorically on catalyst/solvent and continuously on temperature and residence time. I expect at least one catalyst–solvent combination at moderate elevated temperature to improve target yield without strong degradation. Initial batches will screen categories; later batches will refine the best observed recipe. This claim will be changed if final assays show no practically resolvable differences.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
A phase extraction followed by retaining the organic phase and washing it may raise purity, but excessive washing may sacrifice recovery. I will compare extraction and wash choices while remembering that `separate_phase` destroys the unnamed phase. Final decisions require purity >=0.80 and then favor recovery.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [supported only qualitatively; narrowed]
Catalyst/solvent categories materially change reaction and final outcomes, but no screened recipe met the purity constraint. C1-containing aqueous-retained processes gave the strongest recovery among later screens: batch 8 final assay (event runner-operation-0116) gave recovery 0.128 and purity 0.622, while its partial replicate/variant batch 12 (runner-operation-0168) gave 0.110 and 0.589. Differences may include temperature/time and stochastic assay noise, so exact factor attribution remains unresolved.

## H2 [revised]
The assumption that organic retention is generally preferred is not supported. Under the tested conditions, aqueous retention with C1 gave better recovery than corresponding organic-retained screens; extraction category and reaction recipe remain confounded. Organic washing did not rescue purity and sometimes coincided with severe recovery loss (batch 5 final event runner-operation-0077). This does not isolate a causal wash penalty because reaction severity and phase choice differed.

## Decision
No completed batch achieved purity >=0.80. I will recommend batch 8 as the best observed compromise because it had the campaign's highest final recovery while also the highest observed final purity among the stronger-recovery candidates. I would change this decision if repeat evidence showed another batch meeting the purity threshold or exceeding batch 8 recovery at comparable purity.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–partition–purification system rather than a single reaction whose final assay directly reports reactor performance. The limiting reagent first forms target product and competing byproducts; subsequent phase operations redistribute those species, and washing, drying, concentration, sampling, and phase selection alter what reaches the final assay.

A minimal conceptual reaction network is

R → P,  rate kP(C,S,T)[R]
R → B,  rate kB(C,S,T)[R]
P → D,  rate kD(C,S,T)[P]

where R is reagent, P target, B competing byproduct, D degradation material, C is catalyst category, S is solvent category, and T is temperature. A useful phenomenological form would be k_j(C,S,T)=A_j(C,S) exp(-E_j(C,S)/(RT)), but the campaign cannot identify Arrhenius parameters. Residence time increases conversion but can also increase B or D, so maximum conversion need not maximize recoverable target.

After quench, I model extraction approximately through species-specific distribution coefficients. For species i,

f_i,organic ≈ K_i(X,S) Vorganic / (K_i(X,S) Vorganic + Vaqueous),

with the retained aqueous fraction approximately 1-f_i,organic. X denotes extractant category. Final recovery is approximately the amount of P in the retained, processed phase divided by the original 0.04 mol reagent charge. Final purity is P divided by all retained solutes. A wash can be represented by multiplying each retained species by a species-dependent retention factor; it improves purity only when impurity retention is lower than target retention. Drying and concentration mostly remove liquid, although long processing may also cause loss or degradation.

## Evidence that reaction and downstream assays describe different material

The most important interpretive change came from comparing in-process HPLC with final assays. They cannot be treated as repeated measurements of an unchanged sample.

Batch 2, for example, used C1/S1 at 345 K for 3600 s. Reaction-stage HPLC reported conversion 0.243, yield 0.144, selectivity 0.571, purity 0.633, and recovery 0.106. After X1 extraction, retention of the organic phase, drying, and final assay, the reported conversion was 1.000 but recovery only 0.0446, selectivity 0.0323, and purity 0.718. The apparent rise to complete conversion is not credible as ordinary post-quench reaction progress accompanied by such a large target loss. A more coherent explanation is phase conditioning: reactant largely remained in the discarded phase, so the selected organic phase appeared depleted in reactant, while most target was also lost. Thus final conversion is strongly affected by partition and sample domain.

The same pattern occurred in several organic-retained batches: batch 1 had final conversion 0.995 but recovery reported as 0; batch 3 had conversion 0.993 and recovery 0.0280; batch 4 had conversion 1.000 and recovery 0.0226; and batch 7 had conversion 0.998 and recovery 0.0534. By contrast, aqueous-retained batches had more moderate final conversions: 0.188 in batch 6, 0.489 in batch 8, 0.265 in batch 10, and 0.375 in batch 12. I therefore regard final conversion as a selected-phase diagnostic, not a direct estimate of whole-reactor conversion.

## Reaction-category effects

Catalyst and solvent categories clearly mattered, but most early comparisons changed several factors simultaneously, so their individual effects are only partly identifiable.

The early reaction-stage HPLC screens were:

- Batch 1, C0/S0, 360 K for 1800 s: conversion 0.138, yield 0.0508, selectivity 0.418, purity 0.371.
- Batch 2, C1/S1, 345 K for 3600 s: conversion 0.243, yield 0.144, selectivity 0.571, purity 0.633.
- Batch 3, C2/S2, 330 K for 7200 s: conversion 0.291, yield 0.0830, selectivity 0.305, purity 0.332.
- Batch 4, C3/S0, 360 K for 3600 s: conversion 0.214, yield 0.0829, selectivity 0.443, purity 0.486.
- Batch 5, C1/S0, 390 K for 7200 s: conversion 0.604, yield 0.267, selectivity 0.479, purity 0.552.

These observations support three limited conclusions. First, greater thermal exposure generally increased conversion: batch 5 had the largest observed reaction-stage conversion and yield. Second, increased conversion did not guarantee high selectivity or a good isolated product. Third, C1 participated in all of the strongest target-recovery outcomes, although its effect is confounded with solvent, temperature, and phase choice. C2 and C3 were weaker in the tested combinations, but the data do not prove that those catalysts are intrinsically inferior in every solvent.

A plausible kinetic interpretation is that C1 raises kP effectively, while high temperature and long residence also raise kB or kD. Batch 5 illustrates this tradeoff: its strong reaction-stage yield of 0.267 became final recovery 0.0126 and purity 0.123 after organic extraction and three large washes. That failure could reflect poor X1 partitioning, target loss during washing, temperature-driven byproduct formation, or all three; it cannot be assigned solely to reaction degradation.

## Phase and extraction effects

The campaign changed from routinely retaining organic material to testing aqueous retention because organic isolates repeatedly had high apparent conversion but low recovery. The strongest final outcomes came from retaining the aqueous phase with C1:

- Batch 6, C1/S0/X0, 345 K for 3600 s, aqueous retained: recovery 0.0856, purity 0.590, yield 0.0835, selectivity 0.434.
- Batch 8, C1/S2/X2, 370 K for 5400 s, aqueous retained: recovery 0.1275, purity 0.6216, yield 0.1458, selectivity 0.297.
- Batch 12, C1/S2/X2, 350 K for 5400 s, aqueous retained: recovery 0.1098, purity 0.5886, yield 0.1174, selectivity 0.285.

These results suggest that, for at least the C1/S2/X2 region, target product has substantial aqueous retention or that undesirable species favor the organic phase enough to make aqueous retention advantageous. This is a process-level statement, not a molecular identity claim.

Batch 8 and batch 12 are the nearest comparison in the campaign. Their recorded recipe categories, phase choice, and 5400 s duration were the same, while temperature was 370 versus 350 K. Raising temperature was associated with recovery increasing from 0.1098 to 0.1275, purity from 0.5886 to 0.6216, and yield from 0.1174 to 0.1458. This is consistent with higher kP over that interval. However, there was only one run at each temperature, and the differences may include process variability and assay noise; the comparison does not define a reliable temperature-response curve.

A second approximate temperature comparison gives a tradeoff rather than uniform improvement. Batches 7 and 11 both used C0/S1/X1 with organic retention and 5400 s reaction time, at 370 and 350 K respectively. Batch 7 had greater recovery, 0.0534 versus 0.0334, but lower purity, 0.395 versus 0.432. This supports the idea that temperature accelerates target formation and competing material simultaneously.

The organic-retained results also varied strongly with extraction category and upstream recipe: batch 2 reached the campaign's highest final purity, 0.7178, but recovery was only 0.0446; batch 4 gave purity 0.601 and recovery 0.0226; batch 9 gave purity 0.372 and recovery 0.0635; and batch 11 gave purity 0.432 and recovery 0.0334. No tested extraction produced both high purity and high recovery.

## Washing, drying, and concentration

Washing was not demonstrated to be beneficial under the tested conditions. Batch 5 underwent three 0.04 L washes and finished with purity 0.123 and recovery 0.0126, despite having the best measured pre-workup yield. Batch 1 used a smaller organic volume, a wash, drying, and concentration and ended with purity 0.598 but recovery reported as zero. These observations are compatible with target loss to wash liquid, but they do not isolate a wash effect because the batches differed in reaction severity, solvent, extractant volume, and concentration treatment.

Drying and concentration mainly change volume in the public operational record. They should not intrinsically raise solute purity unless they selectively remove water or volatile contaminants. Concentration can increase assay concentration without increasing recovery, and it can amplify losses if product is unstable. The campaign lacks matched runs that identify these effects independently.

## Final performance landscape

Final recovery and purity for the twelve completed batches were approximately:

1. 0.000, 0.598
2. 0.0446, 0.718
3. 0.0280, 0.442
4. 0.0226, 0.601
5. 0.0126, 0.123
6. 0.0856, 0.590
7. 0.0534, 0.395
8. 0.1275, 0.6216
9. 0.0635, 0.3719
10. 0.0816, 0.4493
11. 0.0334, 0.4324
12. 0.1098, 0.5886

Each pair is recovery followed by purity. No batch met the required purity threshold of 0.80. Batch 2 had the highest observed purity but modest recovery. Batch 8 had the highest recovery and a substantially better purity than most other high-recovery batches, which is why it was selected as the operating recommendation despite not satisfying the constraint.

The data reveal a Pareto-like conflict: aggressive removal of reactant or retention of a narrowly partitioned phase can raise apparent purity or apparent conversion while sacrificing target mass. Conversely, retaining the target-rich aqueous phase improved recovery but left enough other solute to keep purity near 0.6.

## Scope and unidentifiable factors

This account applies only to the anonymous benchmark materials and tested operating ranges. C0–C3, S0–S3, and X0–X3 are categorical identifiers, not chemical identities, so no molecular mechanism, acid/base assignment, or real solvent property should be inferred.

Several effects remain unidentifiable:

1. Catalyst–solvent interactions are confounded in the initial screen.
2. Extractant identity is often confounded with catalyst, solvent, temperature, and retained phase.
3. Organic versus aqueous retention was not randomized in a complete matched factorial design.
4. Wash count and volume were not tested in otherwise identical replicate batches.
5. Most conditions lack true replication, so process variability cannot be separated from treatment effects.
6. Final assay selectivity and conversion are conditioned on the selected downstream sample and should not be substituted for reactor-wide kinetic quantities.
7. The reported degradation-warning channel was generally small and noisy; absence of a warning does not prove absence of target loss.
8. Mass-balance errors were small, generally zero to about 0.0065, but that validates internal accounting more than the proposed kinetic interpretation.

## Plausible alternative explanations

The leading alternative to the parallel-reaction explanation is that reaction selectivity is fairly stable and most observed differences arise from species-dependent partitioning and phase-conditioned assays. This is plausible because organic-retained samples frequently showed almost complete apparent conversion with very low recovery. Another alternative is that some product transforms reversibly or changes reporter response during quench and workup; no structural instrument mapping was public, so this cannot be excluded. A third possibility is that wash operations exchange solutes between a retained phase and an implicit wash phase in a way not captured by the simple single-equilibrium equation.

Overall, the most defensible model is therefore hierarchical: catalyst, solvent, temperature, and time determine a reactor mixture; extractant, phase ratio, mixing, settling, and retained phase determine recovery of each mixture component; washing and finishing then impose further species-dependent retention. The campaign strongly identifies the importance of these couplings, tentatively favors C1/S2 with aqueous retention for recovery, and does not identify any process that satisfies purity ≥0.80.

payload.rationale: The predictions use the sealed campaign's qualitative reaction–partition model and deliberately broad intervals because these recipes extrapolate beyond the tested design. Q01–Q06 charge 0.04 mol reagent but only 0.00025 mol C1, one twentieth of the catalyst used in the campaign. Even at 400 K, I therefore expect low target formation and very low recovery; longer heating should raise recovery but may lower purity through competing reactions. X2 is predicted to recover target into the organic phase somewhat better than X0. Increasing organic extractant volume should increase recovery while co-extracting more impurities, producing a modest purity–recovery tradeoff. Q07–Q12 instead charge only 0.002 mol reagent, restoring the 12.5 mol% catalyst-to-reagent ratio used in the campaign. Their lower substrate concentration and 400 K heating are expected to give substantially greater conversion and cleaner target formation than the concentrated campaign runs, although this is a major extrapolation. Washing is predicted to raise purity while sacrificing some target; two staged 0.01 L washes should be more selective than one 0.02 L wash. Concentration is not expected to change solute ratios greatly, so Q11 and Q12 are nearly equal, with a small possible recovery penalty assigned to concentration. Uncertainty includes unknown concentration dependence, catalyst-loading nonlinearity, organic/aqueous partition coefficients, wash selectivity, finishing losses, and final-assay variability.

payload.report:
1. **Claims supported, contradicted, or left untested**

No instance-specific prior, nominal property dossier, or supplied mechanistic law was provided. The materials were anonymous categories, so all substantive laws were self-developed from campaign observations.

- **Supported qualitatively:** Reaction outcome depends on catalyst, solvent, temperature, and time. Reaction-stage HPLC differed substantially across batches 1–5. For example, batch 1 gave conversion 0.138 and yield 0.0508, whereas batch 5, with greater thermal exposure and a different catalyst/solvent combination, gave conversion 0.604 and yield 0.267. These comparisons support dependence on operating conditions, although they do not separately identify each factor.
- **Supported with limited scope:** Greater thermal exposure can increase target production while also worsening purity or downstream performance. Batch 5 had the strongest pre-workup yield but ended at purity 0.123 and recovery 0.0126. The near-matched batches 7 and 11 also suggested a tradeoff: the 370 K run had higher recovery than the 350 K run, 0.0534 versus 0.0334, but lower purity, 0.395 versus 0.432.
- **Supported tentatively:** C1 was the most promising catalyst category in the tested region. The two strongest recoveries were from C1/S2 aqueous-retained batches 8 and 12: 0.1275 and 0.1098, respectively. This remains conditional on their solvents, temperatures, extraction conditions, and retained phase.
- **Contradicted:** My initial expectation that the organic phase should generally be retained was contradicted. Organic-retained batches frequently showed nearly complete apparent final conversion but poor recovery, including batches 1–4. Aqueous-retained C1 batches 6, 8, and 12 instead produced recoveries of 0.0856, 0.1275, and 0.1098. This evidence changed my interpretation from “organic extraction purifies the target” to “phase-specific partitioning dominates the final result, and the target can substantially favor the aqueous material.”
- **Contradicted or at least not supported:** The expectation that washing would reliably raise purity was not supported. Batch 5 underwent three large washes but finished with purity 0.123 and recovery 0.0126. Because its upstream conditions were also severe, this does not prove that washing caused the failure; it does refute any unconditional wash-benefit law.
- **Supported strongly as an interpretive warning:** Final conversion is not interchangeable with whole-reactor conversion. In batch 2, pre-workup HPLC gave conversion 0.243, but the organic final material gave conversion 1.000 while recovery fell to 0.0446. Similar behavior occurred in batches 1, 3, 4, and 7. This evidence changed my judgment: I treated final conversion as conditioned on the selected material rather than as evidence that reaction continued to completion.
- **Untested:** Arrhenius parameters, reaction orders, individual distribution coefficients, catalyst–solvent interaction terms, and species-specific wash-retention factors were not identified. The campaign also did not test whether drying or concentration chemically degraded the target in a controlled matched comparison.

2. **One additional discriminating experiment**

I would repeat the batch-8 upstream recipe—C1/S2, 370 K, 5400 s—but perform quantitative measurements around a single X2 extraction. I would obtain reaction-stage HPLC immediately after quench, mix and settle with the same phase volumes, then quantitatively assay aliquots from both organic and aqueous phases before disposing of either. The two phase measurements would be converted to amount estimates using their phase volumes, permitting a target, reactant, and byproduct balance. The final selected material would then undergo the usual finishing operations and final assay.

This experiment distinguishes my leading explanation—species-dependent partitioning and sample-domain conditioning—from the main alternative that substantial reaction or degradation occurs during workup.

- If the summed target in both phases approximately matches the post-quench target, while reactant and target show different phase fractions, I would strengthen the partitioning explanation. High apparent conversion in an organic aliquot would then be attributed mainly to reactant exclusion.
- If both phases together contain much less target than the post-quench sample, with corresponding increases in byproduct or degradation signal, I would infer genuine target destruction during extraction, settling, or finishing.
- If target is mostly organic despite the superior recovery of aqueous-retained batches, I would reconsider the simple distribution-coefficient model and suspect that later washing, drying, or assay-domain effects caused the campaign pattern.
- If the phase mass balance is poor without a corresponding measured degradation product, I would suspend both explanations and prioritize an unobserved phase, transfer loss, or calibration mismatch.

Replicates would normally be desirable, but under the stated one-experiment constraint the dual-phase mass balance provides more discrimination than another single final assay.

3. **Unused evidence, weak predictions, and influence of the goal**

The campaign generated raw characterization artifacts, chromatographic peaks, spectra, and uncertainty fields that I did not fully inspect or model. I primarily used processed estimates. Intermediate HPLC measurements were also collected in batches 6–12, but their numerical results were not incorporated into my final quantitative comparison. Detailed time, volume, cost, and risk trajectories were largely unused except for confirming process order and phase disposal. Final assay channels other than purity, recovery, conversion, yield, selectivity, degradation warning, and mass-balance error received little attention.

The least reliable predictions are Q07–Q12. They use only 0.002 mol reagent and therefore explore a much lower substrate concentration than the campaign, even though their catalyst-to-reagent ratio resembles the campaign ratio. My relatively high predicted recoveries and purities depend on an unverified conjecture that dilution suppresses competing chemistry. Q01–Q06 are also uncertain because their catalyst loading is one twentieth of the campaign loading at the same 0.04 mol reagent charge; the assumed catalyst-loading response was never measured. Predictions comparing X0 with X2 and different organic phase volumes are weak because extractant identity, phase ratio, and retained phase were confounded in the campaign. The staged-wash comparison Q09/Q10 and concentration comparison Q11/Q12 are directional extrapolations rather than fitted effects.

Batch 8 is the most defensible recommendation only as the best observed compromise, not as a demonstrated optimum. It failed the required purity threshold, reaching purity 0.6216. Batch 2 had the highest observed purity, 0.7178, but only 0.0446 recovery. Thus no completed recipe satisfied the assigned goal, and extrapolation beyond the tested batches would be required to claim success.

The goal affected evidence collection. Because every batch needed a complete reaction/extraction/purification sequence and final assay, substantial resources were devoted to finishing and closing twelve batches. The search emphasized recovery subject to purity and therefore moved from organic retention toward aqueous retention after early recovery failures. This adaptive choice improved process performance but reduced orthogonality: catalyst, solvent, extractant, temperature, phase choice, and washing were often changed together. A mechanism-focused campaign would instead have used matched controls, phase-pair mass balances, and replicates. I see no conflict between the assigned goal and honestly reporting the evidence, but the optimization objective made causal identification weaker than it could have been.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 8 was the best observed recovery–purity compromise: final recovery about 0.128 and purity about 0.622. No completed batch met the required 0.80 purity threshold, so this selection is explicitly based on the strongest available quantitative outcome rather than claimed constraint satisfaction.
